newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices stay buoyant underpinned by winter demand.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices stay buoyant underpinned by winter demand.

text.p: World oil prices extended recent gains and markets were still underpinned on Wednesday by concerns over the supply of heating oil to Western markets as winter approaches.
London November futures for bellwether Brent crude, traded on the International Petroleum Exchange, closed 24 cents a barrel firmer at $23.19.
This is some $5 above levels at this time last year.
European heating oil prices hit five-year highs after the latest weekly U.S. inventory data released late on Tuesday showed heating oil stocks in the world's biggest market were still very low.
"Everyone is going bananas trying to buy it now," one trader said.
U.S. heating oil markets were the driving force behind Wednesday's gains in world oil prices and October London heating oil futures hit $228 a tonne for the first time since August 1991.

The American Petroleum Institute (API) said in its latest weekly report that stocks of distillates, comprising heating oil and diesel, rose just 300,000 barrels from the previous week to 112 million, far less than traders had expected.
The recent sale of a number of cargoes from the U.S. to Europe has served as a significant brake on the replenishment of U.S. stocks, which are still 19 million barrels below year-ago levels.
"The API numbers were yet again supportive for heating oil," said energy analyst Charles Gray at futures brokers Prudential Bache.
Brokers GNI added: "The distillate build was well below expectations...the weather in Europe has turned colder, which is sparking further concern in the heating oil market."
Traders on Wednesday played down the significance for oil prices of Boris Yeltsin's health problems after concerns about the Russian president helped lift markets on Tuesday.
Yeltsin on Wednesday was given the go-ahead for heart surgery and doctors said they were confident the operation would be successful.
Analysts said a change in the Russian presidency was unlikely to have much impact on oil exports from the country which relies heavily on crude and product revenues for hard currency earnings.
"Oil revenue is extremely important to the cash-strapped economy, so any new leader is unlikely to tinker too much with the industry," said brokers GNI.
